cells.tense: Right now, with your hands in it.
cells.verb: tending what's growing, two things at once, without letting either starve
cells.place: in the place where you're always adjusting a little so the whole thing keeps moving
cells.ask: let one person see what the keeping costs you, and let one thing that's finished stay finished
cells.core:
You're keeping two living things fed at once, and neither one is dying for the other. You don't do it by picking a winner — you do it by noticing, a little at a time, which one needs more today and which one can wait, and then actually giving it. Nothing here is being forced. It's being looked after.

That kind of care tends to be invisible, including to the one doing it. There's room now to let someone see what the tending takes — not to be rescued, just seen — and to let something you've grown all the way reach the point where you can set it down. Done can be a kind of harvest, not a loss.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping two things alive at once, and it isn't costing either of them.

cells.tense: You're already in next month, adjusting for weather that hasn't come.
cells.verb: tending what's growing, two things at once, without letting either starve
cells.place: in the place where you're always adjusting a little so the whole thing keeps moving
cells.ask: picture it already grown, fully, and let that picture be the only thing you change today
cells.core:
You're correcting for a future you can't see yet. Every small adjustment gets made twice — once for what's in front of you and once for what might go wrong later — and the things you're tending are starting to feel the hands more than the care. The balance you're after is real. The constant fixing is what's keeping it out of reach.

The way back isn't to adjust less by willpower. It's to go all the way to the other end: let yourself imagine the thing fully grown, the way it would feel to stand in front of it done, and sit in that long enough for the satisfaction to be real. Care that comes from that place doesn't clutch. It can hold something without squeezing it.
cells.sheetLine: You're fixing things that haven't broken yet.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: tending what's growing, two things at once, without letting either starve
cells.place: in the place where you're always adjusting a little so the whole thing keeps moving
cells.ask: name one thing you still want to see grow, and keep wanting it on purpose — let the tending follow the wanting
cells.core:
The adjusting has stopped. Two things that need looking after are being left to find their own level, and they aren't — one is drying out and the other's gone wild, and you're standing a little way off from both. The hands are off, and whatever took them off is still the thing you're facing instead of the garden.

Don't try to push them back on. Go underneath instead: find the one thing you still, honestly, would like to see come up — and let yourself keep hoping for it, out loud if you can, past the point where hope feels sensible. Care that's running on something you still want doesn't exhaust you. The small adjustments come back on their own.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped tending, and things are finding their own level — not a good one.

cells.tense: You're in the room, writing, with the pen set down beside you.
cells.verb: tending what's growing, two things at once, without letting either starve
cells.place: in the place where you're always adjusting a little so the whole thing keeps moving
cells.ask: say to one person what you've actually been keeping alive, and let one finished thing be called finished
cells.core:
You're already doing this. Two things are being kept in balance that would fall over without you — a little more here, a little less there, every day — and when anyone mentions it you say you're just keeping up, or that it's working out on its own. It isn't. Someone is tending it. You'd just rather not be the one named.

The simpler move is underneath the modesty: let the care be visible. Tell one person, plainly, what you're looking after and what it takes. And where something you've grown is actually done, say so, and set it down. When the tending has a name on it, it stops having to be endless.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping this alive. You keep calling it luck.
